clinicalPearls: A low serum calcium in the newborn, conventionally divided into early (first days) and late (end of the first week or later) onset
Early hypocalcaemia is associated with prematurity, maternal diabetes, growth restriction and perinatal asphyxia
Late hypocalcaemia is linked to high phosphate intake, hypomagnesaemia, vitamin D deficiency and hypoparathyroidism
It is often asymptomatic but can cause jitteriness, irritability, feeding difficulty, apnoea and seizures
Persistent or refractory hypocalcaemia should prompt consideration of hypomagnesaemia, DiGeorge syndrome and vitamin D disorders
Management corrects calcium (and any magnesium deficiency) and addresses the underlying cause
reference.pathophysiology: At birth the continuous placental calcium supply ceases, and the newborn depends on parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and calcium intake to maintain calcium. Early hypocalcaemia reflects an exaggerated postnatal fall with immature or suppressed parathyroid responses, more marked in preterm, growth-restricted and asphyxiated infants and those of diabetic mothers. Late hypocalcaemia results from factors that impair calcium handling, such as a high phosphate load, magnesium deficiency (which impairs parathyroid hormone secretion and action), vitamin D deficiency, or congenital hypoparathyroidism as in DiGeorge syndrome. Low ionised calcium increases neuromuscular excitability, causing the clinical features.
additionalDifferentials: Vitamin D deficiency or disorders of vitamin D metabolism
Hypoglycaemia (as another cause of jitteriness and seizures)
additionalInvestigations: Parathyroid hormone and vitamin D where persistent
Assessment for DiGeorge syndrome if features suggest it
Glucose and sepsis evaluation for symptomatic infants
redFlags: Refractory hypocalcaemia suggesting hypomagnesaemia or hypoparathyroidism
Features suggesting DiGeorge syndrome (cardiac, dysmorphic, immune)
Cardiac arrhythmia or prolonged QT interval
reference.prognosis: Early hypocalcaemia usually resolves within days with correction and treatment of contributing factors; prognosis of late or persistent hypocalcaemia depends on the underlying cause.
pitfalls: Failing to correct coexisting hypomagnesaemia, without which calcium is hard to normalise
Overlooking DiGeorge syndrome in persistent hypocalcaemia
Confusing the cause of seizures with hypoglycaemia
Giving a high-phosphate feed that perpetuates late hypocalcaemia
management: Give intravenous calcium (calcium gluconate) for symptomatic or severe hypocalcaemia and oral calcium supplementation for milder cases
Correct coexisting hypomagnesaemia with magnesium, as it impairs parathyroid hormone secretion and perpetuates refractory hypocalcaemia
Treat the underlying cause: reduce a high phosphate load, replace vitamin D in deficiency, and manage hypoparathyroidism
Deliver intravenous calcium under cardiac monitoring for seizures or apnoea, watching for bradycardia and extravasation injury
Monitor total and ionised calcium, phosphate and magnesium during correction
Investigate DiGeorge syndrome and vitamin D disorders in persistent or late hypocalcaemia, with genetics referral where a 22q11 deletion is suspected
